name: ความไวต่อสภาพอากาศ
preview_text: ใน TCM สภาพอากาศที่กระตุ้นคุณ และส่วนใดของร่างกายที่คุณรู้สึกได้ บอกเราได้อย่างชัดเจนว่าระบบอวัยวะใดต้องการความช่วยเหลือ คนส่วนใหญ่สังเกตเห็นเปลวไฟที่เกี่ยวข้องกับสภาพอากาศ...
categories: ["ความไวต่อสิ่งแวดล้อมและสภาพอากาศ"]
synonyms: ["Sensitivity to weather changes", "Symptoms worsen in damp or rainy weather", "Symptoms worsen in damp or windy weather", "Weather-related flare-ups"]
conventional_description: Western medicine recognizes that some people are more sensitive to weather changes, particularly those with conditions like fibromyalgia, arthritis, migraine, or asthma. Symptoms may include joint pain before rain, headaches with barometric pressure shifts, or nasal congestion in cold air. It's often seen as a symptom of an underlying condition rather than a standalone diagnosis, and the exact mechanisms are not fully understood - theories involve changes in barometric pressure, humidity, and temperature affecting tissues and nerve sensitivity.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management typically focuses on treating the underlying condition (e.g., pain relievers for arthritis, inhalers for asthma) and avoiding triggers. Patients are often advised to dress appropriately for the weather, use humidifiers or dehumidifiers, and take antihistamines if allergic rhinitis is involved. There is no specific medication for weather sensitivity itself.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, your body has a protective layer called Wei Qi - think of it as an energetic shield that circulates just under your skin. The Lungs are in charge of spreading this shield. When Lung Qi is strong, you barely notice a change in the weather. But when Lung Qi is weak, even a light breeze can slip through, triggering sneezing, a runny nose, and a general sense of vulnerability.
The Spleen handles moisture. If your Spleen is sluggish, fluids build up inside as dampness - a heavy, sticky residue. When the weather turns damp or humid, that external dampness piles onto your internal dampness, and the Spleen becomes overwhelmed. You feel even heavier, stuffier, and more fatigued. This is why some people dread rainy days: their Spleen is already struggling to keep things dry.
Kidney Yang is like the pilot light that warms your whole body. When it's dim, you feel cold from the inside out, and your lower back and knees ache. Cold or damp weather easily penetrates because there's not enough internal fire to push it back. This deep-level deficiency often underlies chronic weather sensitivity, especially in older adults or after long illness.
Sometimes an acute invasion - a blast of cold wind or a stretch of damp weather - can overwhelm even a relatively healthy person. Wind-Cold attacks the Lungs and causes sudden sneezing and chills; Dampness invades the channels and makes joints heavy and stiff. TCM sees all these patterns not as separate diseases but as different expressions of the same core problem: a mismatch between your inner environment and the outer one.
classical_quote: 「太阳病，发热，汗出，恶风，脉缓者，名为中风。」
classical_translation: "In Tai Yang disease, when there is fever, sweating, aversion to wind, and a moderate pulse, it is called wind strike. This describes the body's defensive Qi being too weak to resist external wind, a core mechanism behind weather sensitivity."
classical_source:
Shang Han Lun (On Cold Damage)  ,  Tai Yang Disease, Line 2 									·
More references
tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what kind of weather triggers your symptoms and what the discomfort feels like. They also note whether the trouble is mainly in the nose and lungs, or if it settles in the joints and muscles. These clues point toward different underlying patterns, and the tongue and pulse help confirm the picture.
If damp or humid days leave you feeling heavy, sluggish, and stuffy, with a poor appetite and a thick, greasy tongue coating, the pattern is likely Spleen Deficiency with Dampness. The weak Spleen fails to manage fluids, so internal dampness makes you react strongly to external damp. The pulse tends to be soft or slippery, and the nasal discharge is often clear or white and persistent.
When cold weather triggers deep chills, low‑back soreness, frequent urination, and a runny nose with clear, watery discharge, Kidney Yang Deficiency is the probable root. The tongue is usually pale and swollen, and the pulse feels deep and weak. This pattern reflects a lack of warming fire at the body’s core, so the person feels cold to the bone and struggles to stay warm even with extra layers.
A person with Lung Qi Deficiency catches every draft. Even a mild breeze or a slight temperature drop brings on sneezing, a runny nose, and sometimes shortness of breath. The tongue is pale, the pulse is weak, and there may be spontaneous sweating. The protective Qi at the skin and nose is simply too thin, so the body cannot shield itself from ordinary weather shifts.
An acute Wind‑Cold invasion shows up as a sudden flare after exposure to a cold wind. Chills, sneezing, and watery nasal discharge appear quickly, often with a stiff neck and body aches. The tongue coating is thin and white, and the pulse is floating and tight. This pattern often lands on top of a chronic deficiency, like a storm hitting an already weakened roof.
When rainy or damp weather brings joint heaviness, stiffness, and aching rather than nasal symptoms, the pattern is Dampness invading the Channels, joints and muscles. The tongue coating is greasy, and the pulse may feel slippery or soft. The discomfort moves with the weather and improves when conditions dry out, pointing to external dampness that has lodged in the channels.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen transforms food and fluids into Qi. When it is weak, fluids accumulate as internal dampness, making the body heavy and sluggish. This internal dampness mirrors external damp weather, so when humidity rises or the weather turns damp, the Spleen becomes overwhelmed, triggering a flare-up of symptoms like nasal congestion, fatigue, and a heavy head.

patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods and avoid raw, cold, or greasy items that produce dampness. Incorporate warming spices like ginger and cinnamon. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps Qi circulate and transforms dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens: Kidney Yang is the body's deep pilot light - it warms every organ and powers the defensive Qi that shields you from wind and cold. When that fire dims, your inner thermostat fails. Cold or damp weather easily penetrates your body because there is not enough warming Yang to repel it, causing chills that settle deep in your lower back and knees, a runny nose with clear, watery discharge, and a dragging fatigue that makes you want to stay bundled up.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a wet white coating. Pulse: deep, slow, and weak, especially at the Chi (third) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney Yang is the body's warming fire. Cold and dampness act like water poured onto embers - they extinguish what little Yang remains, deepening chills and fatigue. Warmth, both external and from cooked foods, feeds that fire directly. Rest conserves the deep energy stored in the Kidneys, while overwork and exposure to cold drain it further. Gentle movement keeps Qi moving without straining the already depleted Yang.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep your lower back and feet warm - a hot water bottle or warming belt can make a big difference. Favor cooked, warming foods like lamb, walnuts, ginger, and cinnamon; avoid raw, cold, or icy foods and drinks. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps circulate Yang without draining it. A short moxibustion session at home on the low back or below the navel can be especially comforting in cold seasons.

patterns.why_this_happens: Your Lungs are responsible for spreading a protective shield of Qi (called Wei Qi) across your skin and nose. When Lung Qi is weak, that shield is thin, so your body can't adapt to even small shifts in wind, temperature, or humidity. The nose is the opening of the Lungs, so weather changes easily trigger sneezing, a runny nose with clear mucus, and that heavy, tired feeling. You may also feel short of breath after mild activity because the Lungs struggle to gather enough Qi.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, tender body with possible teeth marks and a thin white coating. Pulse: empty or weak, especially at the right Cun position (Lung position).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Qi is the source of Wei Qi, the protective energy that circulates at the skin. Cold, dampness, and overexertion drain this Qi, leaving you vulnerable to weather changes. Warmth, rest, and nourishing foods help preserve and replenish Lung Qi, while gentle movement strengthens it without depleting it. Protecting the neck and chest blocks the entry points where wind invades, reducing the trigger for sneezing and runny nose.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congee to support your Qi. Avoid raw, cold foods and icy drinks that chill the Lungs. Gentle movement like walking or Tai Chi helps build Qi without draining it; avoid exhaustive exercise. Keep your neck and chest covered in windy weather, and use a scarf to protect the back of your neck where wind often invades.

patterns.why_this_happens: When a sudden cold wind catches the body off guard, it penetrates the skin and the nose, which are both governed by the Lungs. The invading Cold constricts the Lung's normal ability to diffuse and descend Qi, trapping fluids in the nasal passages and triggering a rapid defensive reaction. This produces the classic acute flare of weather sensitivity: a burst of sneezing, chills, and a flood of clear watery discharge as the body tries to expel the pathogen.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body with a thin white moist coating. Pulse: floating (fu) and tight (jin).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Cold is an exterior pathogen that invades through the skin and nose, constricting the Lung's defensive Qi. Warmth and rest support the body's Yang to push the invader back out, while cold and damp deepen the constriction. Warm fluids and steam help to gently open the pores and nasal passages, restoring the Lung's natural downward and outward flow.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the neck and chest covered when outdoors, and avoid sitting in drafts. Sip warm ginger and scallion tea at the first sign of a chill to help the body sweat lightly and push out the cold. Steer clear of raw salads, iced drinks, and dairy, which can create more internal dampness and phlegm.

patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness is a Yin pathogen that loves moisture and stagnation. Wet weather and cold environments feed it, making joints heavy and stiff. Warmth and dryness act like sunlight after rain - they help evaporate Dampness and get Qi moving again. Gentle movement mechanically pumps the channels, preventing the sticky Dampness from settling, while warm, easy-to-digest foods support the Spleen so it can keep fluids in check.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep joints warm and dry - a scarf or sleeve over affected areas helps. Eat warm, cooked foods like soups and stews, and cut back on dairy, greasy meals, and raw cold foods that breed Dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking or stretching prevents stiffness, but avoid overexertion in wet weather.

faqs.question: Why do I feel so heavy and sluggish when it's damp or rainy?
faqs.answer: In TCM, damp weather easily overwhelms a weak Spleen. Your Spleen is responsible for managing fluids, and when it's already struggling, the external dampness adds to the internal dampness, making you feel heavy, bloated, and tired. The key is to strengthen the Spleen with herbs like Bai Zhu and Fu Ling, and to eat warm, cooked foods that don't create more dampness.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture really help me stop reacting to every cold draft?
faqs.answer: Yes. Acupuncture points like Feishu BL-13 and Lieque LU-7 directly strengthen the Lung Qi and its protective Wei Qi shield. Many people find that after a few sessions, they're less easily triggered by wind and temperature shifts. The effect builds over time, and when combined with herbs like Yu Ping Feng San, the body becomes much more resilient.

faqs.question: How long before I see results?
faqs.answer: Acute flare-ups from a sudden weather change can improve in the first week or two. For chronic sensitivity rooted in deficiency patterns (like weak Spleen or Kidney Yang), expect 2-4 months of consistent treatment to notice a real shift in your baseline reactivity. Most people feel at least some relief after 4-6 sessions, but the goal is to build lasting resilience, not just quick relief.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Yes, diet plays a big role. Cold, raw, and damp-producing foods (like dairy, sugar, and greasy meals) make internal dampness worse, which makes you more sensitive to damp weather. Favor warm, cooked soups and stews, and add a little ginger to your meals. These simple shifts support your Spleen and Lungs between treatments.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my allergy or pain medication?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but always tell both your TCM practitioner and your doctor what you're taking. Herbs like Huang Qi (Astragalus) are safe for most people, but some Blood-moving herbs could interact with anticoagulants. Never stop a prescribed medication without your doctor's guidance, even if you feel better.

faqs.question: What can I do at home between acupuncture sessions?
faqs.answer: Gentle acupressure on points like Zusanli ST-36 (below the knee) and Hegu LI-4 (on the hand) can boost Qi and calm the body. Keep your neck and lower back covered on windy days, and drink warm ginger tea when you feel a chill coming on. These habits reinforce the work your practitioner is doing.

faqs.question: Does weather sensitivity ever go away completely?
faqs.answer: For many people, yes - especially when the root deficiency is addressed. A strong Lung Qi and Spleen can make you far less reactive to weather changes. However, if there's a deep constitutional weakness (like Kidney Yang Deficiency), you may always need to be a little more careful in cold or damp weather, but the severity and frequency of flare-ups can drop dramatically.

research.title: Acupuncture for seasonal allergic rhinitis: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This multicenter RCT compared acupuncture plus rescue medication to sham acupuncture plus rescue medication and rescue medication alone in 422 patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis. Acupuncture significantly improved rhinitis-specific quality of life and reduced antihistamine use over 8 weeks, with benefits persisting into the following pollen season.
research.periodical: Brinkhaus B, Ortiz M, Witt CM, et al. Acupuncture in patients with seasonal allergic rhinitis: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2013;158(4):225-234.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis of 20 RCTs involving 2,356 participants found that Chinese herbal medicine significantly improved nasal symptom scores and quality of life compared to placebo or antihistamines. Formulas like Yu Ping Feng San and Xiao Qing Long Tang were commonly studied, with a favorable safety profile.
research.periodical: Wang S, Tang Q, Qian W, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Evid Based Complement Alternat Med. 2014;2014:857293.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Yu Ping Feng San for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review
research.description: This review analyzed 22 RCTs and concluded that Yu Ping Feng San, alone or combined with conventional therapy, significantly improved symptoms of allergic rhinitis and reduced recurrence rates. The formula was well-tolerated with few adverse events.
research.periodical: Chen Y, Jin X, Yu Z, et al. Yu Ping Feng San for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Complement Ther Med. 2019;43:253-260.
